name: Matterhorn
label: Matterhorn
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/26863664: the OpenStreetMap point 'Matterhorn'.
notes: The iconic pyramid peak that rises above Zermatt.

text.description:
The Matterhorn is the pointed, near-symmetrical peak that towers over Zermatt and is one of the most recognisable mountains in the Alps. Its summit stands at 4,478 metres, and it sits on the border between Switzerland and Italy. It has four steep faces, and the Swiss town of Zermatt lies to the north-east of it. Its shape is so distinctive that many other mountains around the world are nicknamed 'the Matterhorn' of their own country.

It photographs well because nothing crowds the outline. The pyramid shape stands alone above the glaciers and works as a simple, strong subject on a phone screen. The first ascent was made from Zermatt in 1865, and the mountain has drawn visitors ever since the railways arrived in the area at the end of the 19th century. It has also been claimed to be the most photographed mountain in the world.

For your own picture, think of the peak as the subject and look for something nearer to put in front of it, such as rooftops, a fence, a tree or a street lamp. That gives the photo a sense of scale. Leave a little sky above the summit so the tip is not cut off. If cloud is covering the top, wait a few minutes, because it often shifts.
text.geographic_location: The Matterhorn rises to the south-west of Zermatt, in the canton of Valais, and is the mountain that dominates the town's skyline. The mountain overlooks Zermatt.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Zermatt, where the mountain is easy to spot to the south-west. The mountain is visible from around Zermatt, so treat the town and its surroundings as your photo area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (3x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the summit closer and fill the frame. Use the default lens (1x) when you want some of the town or foreground in the picture. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you have a strong foreground, as it makes the peak look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mürini (top of the Mürini hill in Le Petit Village, northeast edge of town; the official site calls it Viewpoint Riedweg). The wooden chalets of the village in the foreground with the Matterhorn rising above them, the classic village-and-peak composition. For your photo, take the mountain's position as the direction to aim at: from Zermatt town, look south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the summit on one of the upper intersections, with the base of the mountain on the lower line. Add a foreground such as a rooftop, fence or tree to give depth. Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot from the same spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so bright snow and sky keep their detail. If your phone offers it, a Live Photo can help you pick the moment when the clouds clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the weather forecast and choose a clear moment, and be ready to wait if cloud is covering the summit.

text.access_note: Check local rules and official guidance for access.

name: Gornergrat
label: Gornergrat
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/434306780: the OpenStreetMap point 'Gornergrat'.
notes: Famous 3,089 m viewpoint with panoramas of the Matterhorn and Monte Rosa.

text.description: Gornergrat is a rocky ridge in the Pennine Alps, 3,135 m high, looking over the Gorner Glacier to the south-east of Zermatt. It photographs well because so much of the high Alps is in front of you at once. The ridge sits between the Gorner and Findel glaciers and has views of 29 mountains over 4,000 m, including the Matterhorn, Monte Rosa's Dufourspitze, Liskamm, Dom and Weisshorn. Gornergrat can be reached from Zermatt by the Gornergrat rack railway, which opened in 1898 and is the highest open-air railway in Europe. It climbs almost 1,500 m from Zermatt. Near the top you will also see the Kulm Hotel, whose two towers have housed astronomical observatories since the late 1960s, which makes a good second subject. For phone photos, start with a wide view of the glacier and the peaks, then move in on single mountains. Look for something in the foreground, such as the rock of the ridge, the railing or a fellow traveller, to give a sense of scale. The air is thin and the light is bright, so check each shot on screen. Mountain weather changes quickly, so take a few frames whenever the peaks clear instead of waiting for a perfect moment.
text.geographic_location: Gornergrat is a ridge about three kilometres east of Zermatt, high above the village, between the Gorner and Findel glaciers. The railway station and the Kulm Hotel sit at its south-western end.
text.directions_text: Start in Zermatt and take the Gornergrat rack railway up to the Gornergrat station, which is the last stop on the line. The phone icon on the map is at the Gornergrat spot itself, so once you are up there you only need to find a clear spot with a view. Check the official railway site before you go for running times and ticket details. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the glacier and the whole line of peaks, the default lens (1x) for a natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Matterhorn or other summits.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You are at the Gornergrat spot itself, so the subject is right where you are. Face the mountains and glacier and move a few steps along the ridge to find a view that is not blocked by people or buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line so the peaks fill most of the frame. Include some ridge rock in the foreground for depth. Zoom in for a tighter shot of the Matterhorn, and try panorama mode for the full sweep, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mountain to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so snow and glacier keep their detail instead of turning plain white. Hold the phone with both hands, as the wind can shake it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Clear mornings are often the best bet, before cloud builds around the peaks, but conditions change a lot, so check the weather forecast on the day.

text.access_note: Gornergrat is reached by a railway that is likely to be ticketed, so check the official site before you go for times and ticket details.
claims_not_in_sources: Mountain weather can change quickly and cloud often builds around the peaks later in the day.
Clear mornings are often the best time for views.
Wind and bright snow glare can affect phone photos at this height.
The railway is likely to be ticketed and run on a timetable, so visitors should check the official site.

name: Zermatt railway station
label: Zermatt Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kirchplatz' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kirchplatz' (way/569953028): middle (42 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Arrival point of the Matterhorn Gotthard Bahn in the car-free village.

text.description:
Zermatt railway station is the southern end of the metre-gauge line up from Visp and Brig, and for most visitors it is the first place they set foot in the car-free village. Several Glacier Express trains start or finish here each day, and a shuttle runs to nearby Täsch every twenty minutes, so there is usually a train coming or going. The Gornergrat Railway's valley station is directly across the street, which makes this a busy spot for arrival-day photos.

Guides call this the classic first Matterhorn photo for new arrivals. From the church steps or the Community Centre terrace, looking south, the Matterhorn rises above the old wooden Valais houses in the foreground. That mix of dark timber and a big peak is what makes the picture work. The station building is not the focus of this view, so think of this as your arrival-day Matterhorn shot, with the station a short walk east.

If you also want the station itself, take a few frames when you pass it. Trains and platform scenes give a good sense of how you arrived. If you would like a second Matterhorn view afterwards, try the river bridge, Kirchbrücke, where the peak is framed down the main street.
text.geographic_location: In Zermatt, in the Canton of Valais, at the foot of Bahnhofstrasse. The station sits directly across the street from the Gornergrat Railway's valley station.
text.directions_text: Zermatt is car-free, so you arrive by train: the Matterhorn Gotthard Bahn runs from Visp and Brig, and a shuttle runs from Täsch. From Zermatt railway station, walk up Bahnhofstrasse to Kirchplatz. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the Matterhorn and the wooden houses sit together in one frame. If the peak looks small, step up to 2x or 3x (depending on your phone) to bring it closer. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the station front or platforms, where you can't step back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kirchplatz (on the church steps or the Community Centre terrace, looking south). The Matterhorn rising above the old wooden Valais houses in the foreground; the sources do not say the station building itself is in frame. Stand on the church steps or on the Community Centre terrace and face south. The Matterhorn rises above the old wooden Valais houses. The station is a short walk to the east, to your left as you face south, and is not what you are framing here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the Matterhorn on one of the upper intersections, with the timber houses filling the lower part of the picture. Keep the phone level so the roofs don't slope. For a second view, Kirchbrücke frames the Matterhorn down the main street from the river bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and snow keep their detail. Live Photos can add a nice touch if people or trains are moving through the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the steps. The peak can be hidden by cloud, so if it is covered, wait a few minutes and check again.

text.access_note: Kirchplatz and the Community Centre terrace are open to the public, and the station is a working railway station, so check the official site before you go for any access or filming restrictions on platforms.
claims_not_in_sources: The station building is not the main subject in the view from Kirchplatz, and the station lies roughly east of the stand-here point.
Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
The Matterhorn can be hidden by cloud at times.
Dropping the exposure slider slightly helps keep detail in bright sky and snow.

name: Zermatt–Sunnegga Funicular
label: Sunnegga Funicular
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q18390964: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Underground funicular to the Sunnegga viewpoint above Zermatt.

text.description:
The Sunnegga funicular links Zermatt village with Sunnegga and the Sunnegga Paradise ski area. It runs underground, so there is no long line of track to photograph. The picture here is the station in its village setting, with people arriving or heading up for the mountains. That makes it a good "getting around Zermatt" shot rather than a postcard view.

A few facts help with captions. The railway climbs 698 m to the top station at 2293 m, and it is the first link on the way to the Sunnegga Paradise ski area. It was heavily modernised by Doppelmayr in 2013. Zermatt Bergbahnen AG has run it since 2002.

For your photo, look for clean lines at the station entrance and signs, with a bit of village street around them. Keep people moving through the frame rather than blocking the doorway. Wipe your phone lens before you start, because Zermatt can be cold and damp. If you want a keepsake of the trip up, take a quick photo of the station name sign as a reminder of where you started.
text.geographic_location: In the resort village of Zermatt, where the lower station of the funicular stands, about 280 m south-west of the stand-here point.
text.directions_text: It is a short walk of about 282 m to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the entrance. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow and you want to include the whole entrance. Use the telephoto (2x or more) for signs and details from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (valley station entrance, Vispastrasse 34 side). The Zermatt valley station of the underground funicular, photographed from the approach in front of the station entrance. Then walk the short distance south-west towards the station for the close-up. The station itself is underground, so you will only see the entrance and building around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the entrance up with a vertical grid line so the building stands straight. Leave space around it for the street. Wait for a gap in the crowd, or let a few people walk through to show scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the entrance to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or snow is washing out. Indoor and underground areas can look dark, so tap on a darker area and check the result.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon is usually quieter. Check the opening times for the funicular on the official site.

text.access_note: The funicular is a working transport line and may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The funicular is a working transport line that visitors may need a ticket to use.
The station entrance is at street level in the village and can be photographed from outside.
Zermatt can be cold and damp, which can mist a phone lens.
Early morning and late afternoon are usually quieter around the station.
The station entrance has a name sign that can be photographed.

name: Gornergrat Railway
label: Gornergrat Bahn
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Riffelalp' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Riffelalp' (node/3444469294): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/548320: large area 'Gornergratbahn' (5554 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Red cog railway climbing from the village to Gornergrat.

text.description:
The Gornergrat Railway is the cogwheel line that climbs from Zermatt to the Gornergrat summit, and it makes a good photo subject in its own right. It opened on 20 August 1898 and was the first electric rack railway built in Switzerland. The line is about 9.3 km long and rises nearly 1,470 m, ending at 3,089 m, which makes it the second highest railway in Europe. That climb is why the train so often has big mountains behind it.

For a picture of the train itself, the Riffelalp stop is a good place to try. A cogwheel train standing at or arriving at the platform, with the Matterhorn behind, gives you a clear story in one frame: the train, the mountain and the sense of height. Railway photographers have tagged this stop, and one guide says the stretch between Riffelalp and Riffelberg is the best for photos from the train. It is a less certain tip than the Golden Spot, so have a look around when you arrive.

The Golden Spot is the other option. It shows the gold-coated historic locomotive 3003 in the foreground with the Matterhorn behind it.

Be flexible with timing. Trains come and go, so wait for one to roll in rather than rushing the shot. The railway usually closes for maintenance in November, and the last descent can be earlier than you expect, so check the timetable before you plan your day.
text.geographic_location: The line starts in Zermatt village, at 1,604 m, and climbs the mountainside to the Gornergrat summit. The Riffelalp stop sits on that climb, well above the village.
text.directions_text: Start in Zermatt and take the Gornergrat Railway up the mountain to the Riffelalp stop, which is a passenger stop on the line. Check the timetable on the official site before you go, so you know when trains run and when the last one comes back down. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the train at the platform with the Matterhorn behind. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), it makes the mountain look larger behind the train. The ultra-wide (0.5x) takes in the whole station, but the Matterhorn will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (at the Riffelalp station on the cogwheel line). A cogwheel train standing or arriving at the Riffelalp stop with the Matterhorn in the background. From here you can photograph a cogwheel train standing at or arriving at the stop, with the Matterhorn in the background. Keep well back from the track edge and stay behind the platform line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the train on one third of the frame, with the Matterhorn rising behind it. Keep the horizon level and leave a little space ahead of the train so it looks as if it is moving into the frame. If you want the gold locomotive in the foreground with the Matterhorn behind, the Golden Spot is the alternative viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the train to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky and snow don't wash out. Turn Live Photos on as you take the shot of an arriving train, so you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the forecast and go on a clear day, when the Matterhorn is visible. Check the timetable first, because the railway usually closes for maintenance in November.

text.access_note: The Riffelalp stop is on a working railway line, so travel is ticketed and the line is subject to timetables and seasonal closures: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Trains stop at the platform and arrive at intervals, so you can wait for one to come in.
Stay behind the platform line near the track edge for safety.
A telephoto lens on a phone makes the background mountain look larger relative to the train.

name: Riffelsee
label: Riffelsee
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Unterer Riffelsee' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/34291839: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Riffelsee' (115 m across).
notes: Mountain lake known for its mirror image of the Matterhorn.

text.description: The Unterer Riffelsee is the smaller, lower neighbour of the Riffelsee, the alpine lake above Zermatt that sits below the Riffelhorn at 2757 m. On a calm day the Matterhorn is mirrored in the water, with rocks along the edge to give the picture a foreground. Guides describe the lower lake as the quieter option. Its sheltered hollow often stays still when the upper lake already has ripples, and it usually has fewer people around. The upper Riffelsee covers just 0.45 ha, so both lakes are small and the reflection depends on very still water. The upper lake shows the Matterhorn's east and northeast faces mirrored, with its rocky edge in front, and it is where the phone icon on the map is placed. The Riffelsee is reached from Rotenboden station on the Gornergrat Bahn, at 2815 m, and the lower lake is about 5 minutes further down the path. The reflection only works when the water is calm and unfrozen. Early morning gives the best chance, and the lakes are frozen in winter and early spring, so there is no reflection then. Even in summer it may not appear on a given day, so try on more than one day if you can. The area is a nature protection zone, so keep to the paths. Check the drone rules if you are thinking of flying one.
text.geographic_location: High above Zermatt, at the Riffelsee, which lies under the Riffelhorn. The nearest station is Rotenboden on the Gornergrat Bahn. The lower lake is about 5 minutes further down the Riffelalp path.
text.directions_text: Take the Gornergrat Bahn to Rotenboden station. From there, follow the Riffelseeweg (trail no. 21) for about 10 minutes to the Riffelsee. The lower lake is about 5 minutes further down on the Riffelalp path. Check the name of the lower lake on the map before you set off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the Matterhorn and its reflection fit in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the rocky edge in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out just the peak and its mirror image.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the Matterhorn's east and northeast faces reflected in the water, with the rocky edge in front. The Unterer Riffelsee is a separate, quieter viewpoint about 5 minutes further down the Riffelalp path, and it is the one to try if the upper lake is rippled.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, so the peak and its reflection line up. Crouch low and use the rocks at the water's edge as a foreground. Include some of the lake's edge, because a frame of only mountain and water can look flat. The Unterer Riffelsee, about 5 minutes further down, is a second viewpoint with its own rocky edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far shore or the mountain to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky and snow keep their detail. Take several shots a few seconds apart, as small ripples come and go. Keep your phone steady and avoid touching the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the best chance of still water and a clear reflection. The lake is frozen in winter and early spring, so there is no reflection then.

text.access_note: The Riffelsee area is a nature protection zone reached by the Gornergrat Bahn, so stay on the paths and check the drone rules before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning gives the best chance of calm water for the reflection (guide advice).
The lower lake is usually calmer and quieter than the upper lake (guide advice).
The lower lake's name comes from one guide and may not be labelled the same way on every map.
Using the ultra-wide lens close to the water emphasises the rocky foreground.

name: Schwarzsee (Zermatt)
label: Schwarzsee
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Schwarzsee' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30950380: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Schwarzsee' (127 m across).
notes: Alpine lake and small chapel at the foot of the Matterhorn.

text.description: Schwarzsee (German for "Black Lake") is a very small lake below the Matterhorn, high above Zermatt at about 2,552 m, right beside the cable car station of the same name. The lake covers only about half a hectare, so it is a quick, easy place to photograph. The star of the picture is the little chapel of Maria zum Schnee (Mary of the Snows), which stands on the edge of the water. On a calm day the dark surface gives you the chapel's reflection, with the Matterhorn rising behind it. If there is any breeze, the reflection breaks up, so be ready to wait a few minutes or come back later. Take your time at the water's edge and try the shot in a few different ways: a wide view with chapel, lake and mountain together, and a closer one with just the chapel and its mirror image. If you want a second view, the Zermatt lettering sign is also recommended, with the Matterhorn's peak behind it. Keep in mind that the lake can freeze in winter, and the chapel then sits close to the pistes, so the scene looks quite different from summer. At this height the weather changes fast, so check the sky before you set off and keep your phone lens clean of fingerprints and damp.
text.geographic_location: Schwarzsee lies high above the town of Zermatt, below the Matterhorn, next to the Schwarzsee cable car station. It is not in the town itself but up the mountain, in the Zermatt area of Valais.
text.directions_text: Start in Zermatt itself and take the cable car up towards Schwarzsee (the ride goes via Furi). From the cable car station, the lake and chapel are a short walk away. Check the official site before you go for cable car times and tickets. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the chapel, lake and Matterhorn together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and shoreline, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Matterhorn closer behind the chapel.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the chapel stands at the water's edge, with its reflection in the dark lake and the Matterhorn rising behind it on calm days.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the chapel on one of the lines, with the Matterhorn above it and the reflection filling the lower part of the frame. Hold your phone low, close to the water, to make the reflection larger. For a different view, the Zermatt lettering sign with the Matterhorn's peak behind it is also recommended.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the chapel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky and snow keep their detail. Wait for the water to go still before you shoot, and take a few frames in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the wind is usually calm and the water is glass-like. Late afternoon and golden hour are also recommended.

text.access_note: The lake shore is free to reach, but getting up here needs the cable car from Zermatt, which is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Weather at this height can change quickly.
Holding the phone low to the water makes the reflection look larger in the frame.
Taking several frames in a row helps catch a moment when the water is still.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in bright sky and snow.
Check on the day whether the Matterhorn itself reflects in the lake; the reliable reflection is the chapel's.

name: Rotenboden railway station
label: Rotenboden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Riffelsee' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Riffelsee' (way/34291839): middle (115 m across); moved 25 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3110648199: the OpenStreetMap point 'Rotenboden'.
notes: Gornergrat railway stop with the classic Matterhorn view over Riffelsee.

text.description: Rotenboden is a small station high on the Gornergrat railway, the rack line that climbs from Zermatt to the Gornergrat summit. At 2,815 m it is the second highest open-air railway station in Europe, after the Gornergrat station on the same line. That height is why the views here are so wide and open. The best photo is not taken on the platform but from the Riffelsee, a small lake a short walk downhill. From its shore you can get the station and the Matterhorn in one frame, with the still water in the foreground. When the air is calm, the lake can show the mountain's reflection, which is why this is the classic postcard view. A trail also leaves the station towards the Monte Rosa Hut, across the Gorner Glacier, so you may see walkers setting off. Keep the horizon level and leave space for the water. Include some of the shoreline so the picture feels grounded. If the lake is rippled or covered in snow, the view is still good, but the reflection will be missing. The ground near the station is rocky, high-altitude terrain, so watch your footing while you hold your phone.
text.geographic_location: Rotenboden is in the municipality of Zermatt, on the Gornergrat railway, west of the Gornergrat summit and well above the village. The Riffelsee lies a short walk downhill from the station.
text.directions_text: Take the Gornergrat railway from Zermatt and get off at Rotenboden, checking the current timetable for the trip back. The station is then about 267 m to the north-east of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the lake, the station and the Matterhorn together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring distant details closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Riffelsee (lakeshore reached by a short walk downhill from the station; the lake is a small tarn, not a park, so the kind is a best fit). The station and the Matterhorn in the same frame, with the lake's still surface as foreground. The Matterhorn can share the frame with the station, so look around to see where it sits in your view. Crouch low near the water's edge so the foreground and any reflection fill the lower part of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the water takes up most of the picture. Place the station off-centre and include the Matterhorn if it is visible in the frame. For a different view, walk up to the Rotenboden station itself and shoot the building from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and snow keep their detail. Wait for a calm moment and take a few shots, or try a Live Photo to catch the best frame when the water settles.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the wind rises, is best for a still lake and a clearer reflection.

text.access_note: This is an open outdoor mountain area reached by the Gornergrat railway, which is a ticketed service, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Riffelsee is a small lake a short walk downhill from the station.
The lake can reflect the Matterhorn when the air is still, and the best conditions are usually early morning before the wind rises.
The reflection is usually only visible in summer, and the lake is often snow-covered in winter.
The ground around the station and lake is rocky, high-altitude terrain where care is needed.

name: Matterhorn Museum
label: Matterhorn Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1385837071: the OpenStreetMap point 'Matterhorn Museum'.
notes: Underground museum on the history of Zermatt and the Matterhorn.

text.description:
The Matterhorn Museum is built to look like a small mountain village, which makes it more fun to photograph than a typical museum. It has 14 houses, including a church, a hotel, huts and granaries, all gathered together to tell the story of the Matterhorn and of how tourism grew up around Zermatt. The museum also tells the story of the first ascent of the Matterhorn by Edward Whymper and his party. One of the more unusual objects is a stone from the summit. Astronaut Claude Nicollier carried two of them into space on the Space Shuttle Endeavour in 1993, and one is on display here. The other was returned to the top of the mountain.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is in the details: old timber walls, small huts, and the contrast between the village buildings and the displays inside. Start with a wide shot to show how the buildings sit together, then move closer to pick out textures such as weathered wood and stone. Indoors, light is usually low and mixed, so hold the phone steady against your body, tap on the brightest object to focus, and nudge the exposure slider down if windows blow out. Check the museum's own rules on photography inside before you go, and keep other visitors out of the frame where you can.

text.directions_text: Open the map and head to the museum, which is the phone icon on the map. Navigate to the museum itself rather than following a fixed route. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of the buildings and displays. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit a whole group of houses into one frame, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved wood, signs and small objects in cases.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your first photo from here, then move around the buildings for different angles.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the walls straight so the old timber buildings do not lean. Include a doorway or window as a frame within the frame. Take one wide shot to show the village-style layout, then a few close-ups of details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on your main subject and slide the exposure down a little if bright windows or sky are washing out the picture. Indoors, hold the phone steady with both hands, or brace it against a wall or your body, and let night mode work if the phone offers it. Avoid flash near displays.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outside, soft daylight (morning or late afternoon) is kinder to wood and stone than harsh midday sun. Inside, the time of day matters less, but quieter periods make it easier to take photos without other visitors in the frame.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so access, opening times and photography rules may be restricted; check the official site before you go.
